ELDER AND DEPENDENT ADULT FINANCIAL ABUSE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan T. Reyes · Pat M. Alvarez

PURPOSE OF THIS ELDER AND DEPENDENT ADULT FINANCIAL ABUSE INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California's Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act (Welfare and Institutions Code section 15600 et seq.) as it applies to financial abuse specifically — the statutory definitions of “elder” and “dependent adult,” the statutory definition of “financial abuse” and its three alternative prongs, the related statutory definition of “undue influence,” the civil remedies the Act makes available for a financial-abuse claim, the mandated-reporter framework (including a category specific to financial institutions), and the statute of limitations that applies to a financial-abuse damages claim under the Act. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes, whose relationship to Pat M. Alvarez is: Adult child. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference, not a private designation, court filing, petition, or report of abuse, and completing it does not itself determine that Pat M. Alvarez is an “elder” or “dependent adult” within the meaning of the Act, that any specific conduct constitutes financial abuse, or that any specific person committed or suffered financial abuse. This document is also distinct from, and does not overlap with, a conservatorship petition: a conservatorship is a court proceeding that appoints a substitute decision-maker for a person going forward, while the Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act instead defines a category of wrongful conduct and civil remedies for it — a distinct legal question that can arise whether or not anyone is, or ever becomes, subject to a conservatorship.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS OF "ELDER" AND "DEPENDENT ADULT"
The Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act applies only to conduct directed at a person who meets one of two defined statutory categories. Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.27 defines “elder” as any person residing in California who is 65 years of age or older — an age-based, residency-based definition with no additional requirement of incapacity, disability, or vulnerability. Section 15610.23 separately defines “dependent adult” in two independent ways: first, as a person between the ages of 18 and 64 who resides in California and who has physical or mental limitations that restrict their ability to carry out normal activities or to protect their rights — expressly including, without limitation, people with physical or developmental disabilities or people whose physical or mental abilities have diminished because of age; and second, regardless of any disability finding, as any person between 18 and 64 who is admitted as an inpatient to a 24-hour health facility as defined in specified sections of the Health and Safety Code. Whether Pat M. Alvarez meets either statutory definition depends on Pat M. Alvarez's age, California residency, and, for the dependent-adult category, the nature of any limitations or inpatient admission — facts this Information Sheet does not evaluate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Elder” means any person residing in this state, 65 years of age or older."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.27 (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.27 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15610.27.)
  "“Dependent adult” means a person, regardless of whether the person lives independently, between the ages of 18 and 64 years who resides in this state and who has physical or mental limitations that restrict his or her ability to carry out normal activities or to protect his or her rights, including, but not limited to, persons who have physical or developmental disabilities, or whose physical or mental abilities have diminished because of age."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.23(a) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.23(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15610.23.)
  "“Dependent adult” includes any person between the ages of 18 and 64 years who is admitted as an inpatient to a 24-hour health facility, as defined in Sections 1250, 1250.2, and 1250.3 of the Health and Safety Code."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.23(b) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.23(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15610.23.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "elder" and "dependent adult" for purposes of its Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person or situation. This clause cites two different code sections (§ 15610.27, a single subsection, and § 15610.23(a)-(b), two subsections of the same section); the two subsections of § 15610.23 are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. This clause states only the statutory definitions; it does not itself determine that any specific person is an "elder" or "dependent adult" under California law, and it is not a substitute for that determination.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "FINANCIAL ABUSE" — THREE ALTERNATIVE PRONGS
Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.30(a) defines “financial abuse” of an elder or dependent adult as occurring when a person or entity does any one of three alternative things: (1) takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains the elder or dependent adult's real or personal property for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both; (2) assists another person or entity in taking, secreting, appropriating, obtaining, or retaining that property for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both; or (3) takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains — or assists in doing so — the elder or dependent adult's property by undue influence, as separately defined in section 15610.70. These three prongs are independent alternatives; a claim of financial abuse rests on establishing any one of them, not all three. Section 15610.30(b) further provides that a person or entity is deemed to have acted for a wrongful use, for purposes of the first two prongs, if the person or entity took, secreted, appropriated, obtained, or retained the property while knowing or having reason to know that doing so was likely to be harmful to the elder or dependent adult — meaning proof of actual intent to defraud is not the only route to a wrongful-use finding.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) “Financial abuse” of an elder or dependent adult occurs when a person or entity does any of the following: (1) Takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains real or personal property of an elder or dependent adult for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both. (2) Assists in taking, secreting, appropriating, obtaining, or retaining real or personal property of an elder or dependent adult for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both. (3) Takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains, or assists in taking, secreting, appropriating, obtaining, or retaining, real or personal property of an elder or dependent adult by undue influence, as defined in Section 15610.70."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.30(a) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.30(a)(1)-(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15610.30.)
  "(b) A person or entity shall be deemed to have taken, secreted, appropriated, obtained, or retained property for a wrongful use if, among other things, the person or entity takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains the property and the person or entity knew or should have known that this conduct is likely to be harmful to the elder or dependent adult."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.30(b) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.30(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15610.30.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "financial abuse" of an elder or dependent adult, including its three alternative statutory prongs — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific set of facts. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15610.30(a) and (b)); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Subsections (c) and (d) of the same section, defining when property is "taken" for purposes of the statute and defining "representative," are not quoted or described in this clause. This clause states only the statutory definition; it does not itself determine that any specific conduct constitutes financial abuse or that any specific person committed or suffered financial abuse.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "UNDUE INFLUENCE" AND ITS ENUMERATED FACTORS
Where a claim of financial abuse rests on the third statutory prong — taking property “by undue influence” — Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.70, added in 2013, supplies the governing definition; the Act does not leave “undue influence” to be defined by cross-reference to a different code. Section 15610.70(a) defines “undue influence” as “excessive persuasion that causes another person to act or refrain from acting by overcoming that person's free will and results in inequity,” and directs that four categories of evidence be considered in determining whether a result was produced by undue influence: the victim's vulnerability (including incapacity, illness, disability, injury, age, education, impaired cognitive function, emotional distress, isolation, or dependency, and whether the influencer knew or should have known of it); the influencer's apparent authority (including status as a fiduciary, family member, care provider, health care professional, legal professional, or spiritual adviser); the actions or tactics the influencer used (including controlling necessaries of life or access to information, use of affection, intimidation, or coercion, and haste or secrecy in effecting changes); and the equity of the result (including the economic consequences to the victim and any divergence from the victim's prior intent or course of conduct). Section 15610.70(b) adds an express limit: evidence that a result was inequitable, standing alone, is not sufficient to prove undue influence — the other statutory factors must also be considered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) “Undue influence” means excessive persuasion that causes another person to act or refrain from acting by overcoming that person’s free will and results in inequity. In determining whether a result was produced by undue influence, all of the following shall be considered: (1) The vulnerability of the victim. Evidence of vulnerability may include, but is not limited to, incapacity, illness, disability, injury, age, education, impaired cognitive function, emotional distress, isolation, or dependency, and whether the influencer knew or should have known of the alleged victim’s vulnerability. (2) The influencer’s apparent authority. Evidence of apparent authority may include, but is not limited to, status as a fiduciary, family member, care provider, health care professional, legal professional, spiritual adviser, expert, or other qualification. (3) The actions or tactics used by the influencer. Evidence of actions or tactics used may include, but is not limited to, all of the following: (A) Controlling necessaries of life, medication, the victim’s interactions with others, access to information, or sleep. (B) Use of affection, intimidation, or coercion. (C) Initiation of changes in personal or property rights, use of haste or secrecy in effecting those changes, effecting changes at inappropriate times and places, and claims of expertise in effecting changes. (4) The equity of the result. Evidence of the equity of the result may include, but is not limited to, the economic consequences to the victim, any divergence from the victim’s prior intent or course of conduct or dealing, the relationship of the value conveyed to the value of any services or consideration received, or the appropriateness of the change in light of the length and nature of the relationship."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.70(a) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.70(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15610.70.)
  "(b) Evidence of an inequitable result, without more, is not sufficient to prove undue influence."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.70(b) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.70(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15610.70.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "undue influence" for purposes of a financial-abuse claim, and of the factors the statute directs be considered — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific set of facts. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15610.70(a) and (b)); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Research-tool limitation: this clause was researched together with an attempt to locate a citable, verifiable published California appellate decision applying this statutory undue-influence factor list to a financial-abuse claim; the case-law research tool used for this project (CourtListener) returned a daily rate-limit error (125 requests/day exceeded) before any case could be located and independently verified, so no case-law citation is included here — this clause rests on the statutory text alone, and no case law should be assumed to have been checked. This clause states only the statutory definition and factors; it does not itself determine that any specific person exercised undue influence over any other specific person, or that any specific result was produced by undue influence.

CIVIL REMEDIES FOR FINANCIAL ABUSE — ATTORNEY'S FEES AND THE DIFFERENT PROOF STANDARDS THAT APPLY
Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.5 supplies the civil remedies specific to a financial-abuse claim under the Act. This is a separate remedy provision from the Act's general elder-abuse remedy statute, section 15657, which by its own terms applies only to claims of physical abuse, neglect, or abandonment — not financial abuse. Under section 15657.5(a), where a defendant's liability for financial abuse is proven merely by a preponderance of the evidence, the court shall award the plaintiff reasonable attorney's fees and costs, in addition to compensatory damages and all other remedies otherwise provided by law. A higher proof standard applies to one additional, separate remedy: under section 15657.5(b), where financial-abuse liability is proven by a preponderance of the evidence and it is separately proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant acted with recklessness, oppression, fraud, or malice in committing the abuse, the damages limitations that Code of Civil Procedure section 377.34 would otherwise impose on a claim that survives the plaintiff's death do not apply. Attorney's fees and costs under the Act are thus available on an ordinary preponderance-of-the-evidence standard; it is only the removal of the survival-action damages cap that requires clear and convincing evidence of aggravated conduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Where it is proven by a preponderance of the evidence that a defendant is liable for financial abuse, as defined in Section 15610.30, in addition to compensatory damages and all other remedies otherwise provided by law, the court shall award to the plaintiff reasonable attorney’s fees and costs."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15657.5(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15657.5.)
  "(b) Where it is proven by a preponderance of the evidence that a defendant is liable for financial abuse, as defined in Section 15610.30, and where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of recklessness, oppression, fraud, or malice in the commission of the abuse, in addition to reasonable attorney’s fees and costs set forth in subdivision (a), compensatory damages, and all other remedies otherwise provided by law, the limitations imposed by Section 377.34 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the damages recoverable shall not apply."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15657.5(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15657.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the civil remedies California makes available for a financial-abuse claim under the Act and the proof standards that attach to each — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific claim. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15657.5(a) and (b)); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Correction to an initial research assumption: section 15657 does carry a clear-and-convincing evidentiary standard and a structure that resembles section 15657.5's, but section 15657 governs only physical abuse, neglect, and abandonment claims under the Act — as stated on the face of section 15657 itself — and is not an available remedy provision for a financial-abuse claim, which is instead governed exclusively by section 15657.5. This clause does not attach the general section 15657 text as an independent citation because it is describing what section 15657.5, not section 15657, provides; the contrast is stated only in this gap note, drawn from the same verified fetch of section 15657 described in this project's research. Section 15657.5(c)-(e), addressing the separate standard for punitive damages against an employer and a required statement in any resulting money judgment, are not quoted or described in this clause. This clause states only the statutory remedies and proof standards; it does not itself determine that any specific defendant is liable for financial abuse, that any specific defendant acted with recklessness, oppression, fraud, or malice, or that any specific plaintiff is entitled to any remedy.

STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS FOR A FINANCIAL-ABUSE DAMAGES CLAIM — FOUR YEARS FROM DISCOVERY
Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.7 sets a limitations period specific to a financial-abuse damages claim under the Act, distinct from the limitations periods that apply to ordinary tort or contract claims. An action for damages under sections 15657.5 and 15657.6 for financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult, as defined in section 15610.30, must be commenced within four years after the plaintiff discovers, or through the exercise of reasonable diligence should have discovered, the facts constituting the financial abuse. This is a discovery-based period, not a fixed period running automatically from the date of the underlying conduct — the four years runs from when the facts constituting the abuse were, or reasonably should have been, discovered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An action for damages pursuant to Sections 15657.5 and 15657.6 for financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult, as defined in Section 15610.30, shall be commenced within four years after the plaintiff discovers or, through the exercise of reasonable diligence, should have discovered, the facts constituting the financial abuse."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.7 (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15657.7 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15657.7.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the limitations period that applies to a financial-abuse damages claim under California's Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act — not a claim about which state's law, or which limitations period, governs a specific claim, and not a claim about the limitations period for any non-financial-abuse claim (including physical abuse, neglect, or abandonment claims, which section 15657.7 does not govern). This is a single statutory section, and no subsection of it is cited more than once in this clause. This clause states only the statutory limitations period; it does not itself determine when any specific plaintiff discovered or should have discovered any specific facts, or that any specific claim is or is not time-barred.

GENERAL MANDATED-REPORTER CATEGORIES AND REPORTING DUTY (FINANCIAL ABUSE INCLUDED)
Welfare and Institutions Code section 15630 designates broad categories of people as mandated reporters of suspected elder and dependent adult abuse, and financial abuse is expressly included among the abuse types those reporters must report — within section 15630 itself, financial abuse is not treated as a narrower category than physical abuse. Section 15630(a) designates as a mandated reporter any person who has assumed full or intermittent responsibility for the care or custody of an elder or dependent adult, whether or not compensated, including administrators, supervisors, and licensed staff of a facility that provides care or services for elder or dependent adults, any elder or dependent adult care custodian, health practitioner, clergy member, or employee of a county adult protective services agency or a local law enforcement agency. Under section 15630(b)(1), a mandated reporter who, in a professional capacity or within the scope of employment, observes or has knowledge of an incident that reasonably appears to be financial abuse (among other listed abuse types), or reasonably suspects it, must report the known, suspected, or alleged instance by telephone or through a confidential internet reporting tool immediately or as soon as practicably possible; if the report is made by telephone, a written or internet report must follow within two working days. Where the suspected abuse occurred outside a long-term care facility, a state mental hospital, or a state developmental center, section 15630(b)(1)(F) directs that the report be made to the county adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A person who has assumed full or intermittent responsibility for the care or custody of an elder or dependent adult, whether or not they receive compensation, including administrators, supervisors, and any licensed staff of a public or private facility that provides care or services for elder or dependent adults, or any elder or dependent adult care custodian, health practitioner, clergy member, or employee of a county adult protective services agency or a local law enforcement agency, is a mandated reporter."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15630(a) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15630(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15630.)
  "(b) (1) A mandated reporter who, in their professional capacity, or within the scope of their employment, has observed or has knowledge of an incident that reasonably appears to be physical abuse, as defined in Section 15610.63, abandonment, abduction, isolation, financial abuse, or neglect, or is told by an elder or dependent adult that they have experienced behavior, including an act or omission, constituting physical abuse, as defined in Section 15610.63, abandonment, abduction, isolation, financial abuse, or neglect, or reasonably suspects that abuse, shall report the known, suspected, or alleged instance of abuse by telephone or through a confidential internet reporting tool, as authorized by Section 15658, immediately or as soon as practicably possible. If reported by telephone, a written report shall be sent, or an internet report shall be made through the confidential internet reporting tool established in Section 15658, within two working days."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15630(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15630(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15630.)
  "(F) If the abuse has occurred in any place other than a long-term care facility, a state mental hospital, or a state developmental center, the report shall be made to the adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15630(b)(1)(F) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15630(b)(1)(F) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15630.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's general mandated-reporter categories and reporting duty for suspected elder and dependent adult abuse, including financial abuse — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reporter's obligations. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15630(a), (b)(1), and (b)(1)(F)); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Section 15630 is substantially longer than what is quoted or described here — it separately addresses reporting within long-term care facilities, state mental hospitals, and state developmental centers; a narrow exception for clergy members receiving a penitential communication; a narrow exception for certain physicians, registered nurses, and psychotherapists; permissive (non-mandatory) reporting of other abuse types; and criminal penalties for a mandated reporter's willful failure to report — none of which this clause fully describes. A distinct and narrower mandated-reporter category that applies specifically to financial abuse — officers and employees of financial institutions — is addressed separately in this document's companion clause on section 15630.1. This clause does not itself determine that any specific person is a mandated reporter or that any specific reporter's duty has or has not been triggered.

A NARROWER, FINANCIAL-ABUSE-SPECIFIC MANDATED-REPORTER CATEGORY: FINANCIAL INSTITUTION OFFICERS AND EMPLOYEES
Separate from the general mandated-reporter categories in section 15630, Welfare and Institutions Code section 15630.1 — part of the Financial Elder Abuse Reporting Act of 2005 — creates a mandated-reporter category and reporting duty that exist only for suspected financial abuse, not for other abuse types. Section 15630.1(a) defines a “mandated reporter of suspected financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult” as all officers and employees of financial institutions, a term section 15630.1(b) defines to include depository institutions, institution-affiliated parties, and federal or state credit unions. Under section 15630.1(d)(1), a financial institution officer or employee who has direct contact with an elder or dependent adult, or who reviews or approves that person's financial documents, records, or transactions, and who, within the scope of that employment, observes, has knowledge of, or reasonably suspects an incident of financial abuse, must report the known or suspected instance by telephone or through a confidential internet reporting tool immediately or as soon as practicably possible; a telephone report must be followed by a written or internet report within two working days, to the local adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency. Enforcement of this financial-institution duty differs from enforcement of the general mandated-reporter statute: section 15630.1(f) makes a financial institution's failure to report a civil penalty of up to $1,000 (up to $5,000 if the failure is willful), recoverable only in a civil action brought by the Attorney General, a district attorney, or county counsel — not the misdemeanor criminal penalty that section 15630(h) attaches to a mandated reporter's failure to report under the general statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) As used in this section, “mandated reporter of suspected financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult” means all officers and employees of financial institutions."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15630.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15630.1(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15630.1.)
  "(d) (1) Any mandated reporter of suspected financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult who has direct contact with the elder or dependent adult or who reviews or approves the elder or dependent adult’s financial documents, records, or transactions, in connection with providing financial services with respect to an elder or dependent adult, and who, within the scope of his or her employment or professional practice, has observed or has knowledge of an incident, that is directly related to the transaction or matter that is within that scope of employment or professional practice, that reasonably appears to be financial abuse, or who reasonably suspects that abuse, based solely on the information before him or her at the time of reviewing or approving the document, record, or transaction in the case of mandated reporters who do not have direct contact with the elder or dependent adult, shall report the known or suspected instance of financial abuse by telephone or through a confidential Internet reporting tool, as authorized pursuant to Section 15658, immediately, or as soon as practicably possible. If reported by telephone, a written report shall be sent, or an Internet report shall be made through the confidential Internet reporting tool established in Section 15658, within two working days to the local adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15630.1(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15630.1(d)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15630.1.)
  "(f) Failure to report financial abuse under this section shall be subject to a civil penalty not exceeding one thousand dollars ($1,000) or if the failure to report is willful, a civil penalty not exceeding five thousand dollars ($5,000), which shall be paid by the financial institution that is the employer of the mandated reporter to the party bringing the action."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15630.1(f) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15630.1(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15630.1.)
  "(h) Failure to report, or impeding or inhibiting a report of, physical abuse, as defined in Section 15610.63, abandonment, abduction, isolation, financial abuse, or neglect of an elder or dependent adult, in violation of this section, is a misdemeanor, punishable by not more than six months in the county jail, by a fine of not more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), or by both that fine and imprisonment."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15630(h) (California Legislative Information text), Welf. & Inst. C. § 15630(h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15630.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's Financial Elder Abuse Reporting Act of 2005 creates a mandated-reporter category and reporting duty that exist specifically for financial abuse and apply only to financial institution officers and employees — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reporter's obligations. This clause cites three subsections of section 15630.1 (§ 15630.1(a), (d)(1), and (f)), treated here as one source rather than independent corroborating sources; it also cites one subsection of the separate section 15630 (§ 15630(h)) solely for contrast with section 15630.1(f)'s civil-penalty enforcement mechanism — that single citation is not treated as independent corroboration of anything this clause states about section 15630.1 itself. This clause does not itself determine that any specific officer or employee is a mandated reporter under this section, that any specific transaction or conduct constitutes suspected financial abuse, or that any specific report was or was not required.

Section 15610.23 separately defines “dependent adult” in two independent ways: first, as a person between the ages of 18 and 64 who resides in California and who has physical or mental limitations that restrict their ability to carry out normal activities or to protect their rights — expressly including, without limitation, people with physical or developmental disabilities or people whose physical or mental abilities have diminished because of age; and second, regardless of any disability finding, as any person between 18 and 64 who is admitted as an inpatient to a 24-hour health facility as defined in specified sections of the Health and Safety Code. Whether Pat M. Alvarez meets either statutory definition depends on Pat M. Alvarez's age, California residency, and, for the dependent-adult category, the nature of any limitations or inpatient admission — facts this Information Sheet does not evaluate.

expectedJSON.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.30(a) defines “financial abuse” of an elder or dependent adult as occurring when a person or entity does any one of three alternative things: (1) takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains the elder or dependent adult's real or personal property for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both; (2) assists another person or entity in taking, secreting, appropriating, obtaining, or retaining that property for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both; or (3) takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains — or assists in doing so — the elder or dependent adult's property by undue influence, as separately defined in section 15610.70. These three prongs are independent alternatives; a claim of financial abuse rests on establishing any one of them, not all three. Section 15610.30(b) further provides that a person or entity is deemed to have acted for a wrongful use, for purposes of the first two prongs, if the person or entity took, secreted, appropriated, obtained, or retained the property while knowing or having reason to know that doing so was likely to be harmful to the elder or dependent adult — meaning proof of actual intent to defraud is not the only route to a wrongful-use finding.

expectedJSON.body: Where a claim of financial abuse rests on the third statutory prong — taking property “by undue influence” — Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.70, added in 2013, supplies the governing definition; the Act does not leave “undue influence” to be defined by cross-reference to a different code. Section 15610.70(a) defines “undue influence” as “excessive persuasion that causes another person to act or refrain from acting by overcoming that person's free will and results in inequity,” and directs that four categories of evidence be considered in determining whether a result was produced by undue influence: the victim's vulnerability (including incapacity, illness, disability, injury, age, education, impaired cognitive function, emotional distress, isolation, or dependency, and whether the influencer knew or should have known of it); the influencer's apparent authority (including status as a fiduciary, family member, care provider, health care professional, legal professional, or spiritual adviser); the actions or tactics the influencer used (including controlling necessaries of life or access to information, use of affection, intimidation, or coercion, and haste or secrecy in effecting changes); and the equity of the result (including the economic consequences to the victim and any divergence from the victim's prior intent or course of conduct). Section 15610.70(b) adds an express limit: evidence that a result was inequitable, standing alone, is not sufficient to prove undue influence — the other statutory factors must also be considered.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.70(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) “Undue influence” means excessive persuasion that causes another person to act or refrain from acting by overcoming that person’s free will and results in inequity. In determining whether a result was produced by undue influence, all of the following shall be considered: (1) The vulnerability of the victim. Evidence of vulnerability may include, but is not limited to, incapacity, illness, disability, injury, age, education, impaired cognitive function, emotional distress, isolation, or dependency, and whether the influencer knew or should have known of the alleged victim’s vulnerability. (2) The influencer’s apparent authority. Evidence of apparent authority may include, but is not limited to, status as a fiduciary, family member, care provider, health care professional, legal professional, spiritual adviser, expert, or other qualification. (3) The actions or tactics used by the influencer. Evidence of actions or tactics used may include, but is not limited to, all of the following: (A) Controlling necessaries of life, medication, the victim’s interactions with others, access to information, or sleep. (B) Use of affection, intimidation, or coercion. (C) Initiation of changes in personal or property rights, use of haste or secrecy in effecting those changes, effecting changes at inappropriate times and places, and claims of expertise in effecting changes. (4) The equity of the result. Evidence of the equity of the result may include, but is not limited to, the economic consequences to the victim, any divergence from the victim’s prior intent or course of conduct or dealing, the relationship of the value conveyed to the value of any services or consideration received, or the appropriateness of the change in light of the length and nature of the relationship.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.70(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (b) Evidence of an inequitable result, without more, is not sufficient to prove undue influence.

expectedJSON.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.5 supplies the civil remedies specific to a financial-abuse claim under the Act. This is a separate remedy provision from the Act's general elder-abuse remedy statute, section 15657, which by its own terms applies only to claims of physical abuse, neglect, or abandonment — not financial abuse. Under section 15657.5(a), where a defendant's liability for financial abuse is proven merely by a preponderance of the evidence, the court shall award the plaintiff reasonable attorney's fees and costs, in addition to compensatory damages and all other remedies otherwise provided by law. A higher proof standard applies to one additional, separate remedy: under section 15657.5(b), where financial-abuse liability is proven by a preponderance of the evidence and it is separately proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant acted with recklessness, oppression, fraud, or malice in committing the abuse, the damages limitations that Code of Civil Procedure section 377.34 would otherwise impose on a claim that survives the plaintiff's death do not apply. Attorney's fees and costs under the Act are thus available on an ordinary preponderance-of-the-evidence standard; it is only the removal of the survival-action damages cap that requires clear and convincing evidence of aggravated conduct.

expectedJSON.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15630 designates broad categories of people as mandated reporters of suspected elder and dependent adult abuse, and financial abuse is expressly included among the abuse types those reporters must report — within section 15630 itself, financial abuse is not treated as a narrower category than physical abuse. Section 15630(a) designates as a mandated reporter any person who has assumed full or intermittent responsibility for the care or custody of an elder or dependent adult, whether or not compensated, including administrators, supervisors, and licensed staff of a facility that provides care or services for elder or dependent adults, any elder or dependent adult care custodian, health practitioner, clergy member, or employee of a county adult protective services agency or a local law enforcement agency. Under section 15630(b)(1), a mandated reporter who, in a professional capacity or within the scope of employment, observes or has knowledge of an incident that reasonably appears to be financial abuse (among other listed abuse types), or reasonably suspects it, must report the known, suspected, or alleged instance by telephone or through a confidential internet reporting tool immediately or as soon as practicably possible; if the report is made by telephone, a written or internet report must follow within two working days. Where the suspected abuse occurred outside a long-term care facility, a state mental hospital, or a state developmental center, section 15630(b)(1)(F) directs that the report be made to the county adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency.

expectedJSON.body: Separate from the general mandated-reporter categories in section 15630, Welfare and Institutions Code section 15630.1 — part of the Financial Elder Abuse Reporting Act of 2005 — creates a mandated-reporter category and reporting duty that exist only for suspected financial abuse, not for other abuse types. Section 15630.1(a) defines a “mandated reporter of suspected financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult” as all officers and employees of financial institutions, a term section 15630.1(b) defines to include depository institutions, institution-affiliated parties, and federal or state credit unions. Under section 15630.1(d)(1), a financial institution officer or employee who has direct contact with an elder or dependent adult, or who reviews or approves that person's financial documents, records, or transactions, and who, within the scope of that employment, observes, has knowledge of, or reasonably suspects an incident of financial abuse, must report the known or suspected instance by telephone or through a confidential internet reporting tool immediately or as soon as practicably possible; a telephone report must be followed by a written or internet report within two working days, to the local adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency. Enforcement of this financial-institution duty differs from enforcement of the general mandated-reporter statute: section 15630.1(f) makes a financial institution's failure to report a civil penalty of up to $1,000 (up to $5,000 if the failure is willful), recoverable only in a civil action brought by the Attorney General, a district attorney, or county counsel — not the misdemeanor criminal penalty that section 15630(h) attaches to a mandated reporter's failure to report under the general statute.

If reported by telephone, a written report shall be sent, or an Internet report shall be made through the confidential Internet reporting tool established in Section 15658, within two working days to the local adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency.
